tip: English says 'on foot'; Greek says with the feet – με τα πόδια (me ta pódhia), article included.
Σε (se) + τον (ton) fuse into στον (ston) before masculine nouns: πάω στον φούρνο (páo ston fúrno = I go to the bakery).
Some verbs only exist in the -ομαι (-ome) form: έρχομαι (érkhome = I come). The unusual ending changes nothing – the meaning is a plain action.
City names normally take 'the': από την Αθήνα (apó tin Athína) is literally 'from the Athens'. Countries too – η Ελλάδα (i Elládha).
Clock times are 'at the...': στις εφτά (stis eftá) = at seven. The 'the' is plural because it agrees with the unspoken ώρες (óres = hours).
One present tense does both English ones: δουλεύω (dhulévo) = 'I work' and 'I am working'. Greek has no separate -ing form.
Possession keeps the article and puts 'my' after: τη μητέρα μου (ti mitéra mu) = 'the mother of-me'. As a possessive, μου (mu) follows the noun.
Time of day needs no 'in': το βράδυ (to vrádhi) = in the evening, literally just 'the evening'. Mornings match: το πρωί (to proí).
The future is just θα (tha) + verb: θα πάω (tha páo) = I will go. It never changes – one little word for every person and verb.
Negative future has a fixed order – δεν (dhen) before θα (tha): δεν θα δουλεύω (dhen tha dhulévo = I will not be working).
Liking flips the roles: the thing pleases you – μου αρέσει ο καφές (mu arési o kafés = the coffee pleases me = I like coffee).
Liking flips in Greek: μου αρέσει πολύ το τυρί (mu arési polí to tirí) = 'the cheese pleases me a lot'. You're the receiver, not the doer.
Liking to do something adds να (na) + verb: της αρέσει να μαγειρεύει (tis arési na mayirévi = cooking pleases her = she likes to cook).
Greek has no 'to read' form – after να (na) the verb still conjugates: μου αρέσει να διαβάζω (mu arési na dhiavázo) = 'I like that I read'.
No word for 'by' with cards, just με (me): πλήρωσα με κάρτα (plírosa me kárta = I paid by card).
The event is a one-off, so δοκίμασα (dhokímasa = I tried on); the description keeps the ongoing past: ήταν μικρό (ítan mikró = it was small).
'By herself' agrees with the person: μόνη της (móni tis) for a woman, μόνος του (mónos tu) for a man.
In questions τίποτα (típota) means 'anything': έφαγες τίποτα; (éfayes típota = did you eat anything?)
Liking in the past: μου άρεσε (mu árese = I liked it), literally 'it pleased me'.
Κλείνω (klíno) means both 'close' and 'book': έκλεισα τραπέζι (éklisa trapézi = I booked a table).
Greek stacks negatives: δεν έφαγα τίποτα (dhen éfagha típota = I didn't eat anything) is literally 'not I-ate nothing' – both words are required.
You ask a thing 'from' a person in Greek: ζήτησα από τον σερβιτόρο (zítisa apó ton servitóro = I asked from the waiter).
No 'on' with holidays: πήγαμε διακοπές (píghame dhiakopés = we went on holiday) – διακοπές attaches straight to the verb.
Στην ώρα του = on time, literally 'at its hour': έφυγε στην ώρα του (éfiye stin óra tu).
Booking is closing in Greek: έκλεισα τα εισιτήρια (éklisa ta isitíria = I booked the tickets). Κλείνω (klíno) also books tables and hotel rooms.
Χάνω (kháno) covers both 'lose' and 'miss': χάσαμε το τρένο (khásame to tréno = we missed the train).
Κρατάω (kratáo) also means 'to last': κράτησε τρεις ώρες (krátise tris óres = it lasted three hours).
Μένω (méno) covers both 'live' and 'stay': μείναμε σε ένα μικρό ξενοδοχείο (míname se éna mikró ksenodhokhío = we stayed at a small hotel).
After motion verbs, home needs no 'to' or article: γύρισα σπίτι (yírisa spíti = I returned home) – just the bare word.
A good time 'passes' in Greek: περάσαμε υπέροχα (perásame ipérokha = we passed wonderfully = we had a wonderful time).
